title: Cardio for fat loss and health without killing your gains
chunks: Cardio improves heart health, endurance, and recovery capacity, and it burns extra calories that can support fat loss. It is a useful tool, but for body composition it is a complement to diet and resistance training, not a replacement. You cannot out-cardio a poor diet.

Low-intensity steady-state cardio (LISS) — like brisk walking, easy cycling, or incline treadmill walking — is easy to recover from and barely interferes with lifting. It is excellent for adding to your daily energy expenditure during a cut without adding much fatigue.

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) burns more calories per minute and improves conditioning, but it is far more fatiguing and can cut into leg recovery and lifting performance if overused. Keep HIIT to a couple of short sessions a week and schedule it away from heavy leg days.

Daily steps are one of the most underrated fat-loss tools. Simply walking more increases your non-exercise activity (NEAT) and can burn meaningful calories with almost no recovery cost. A target of around 7,000–10,000 steps a day is a practical, sustainable goal for many people.

If your main goal is muscle, keep cardio modest so it does not eat into recovery — a few short LISS sessions or just walking is usually enough. Long, frequent, intense cardio alongside a calorie surplus can blunt muscle gains and burn the energy meant for growth.

Place cardio to minimize interference: do hard cardio after lifting or on separate days, and keep intense leg-focused cardio away from heavy lower-body sessions. Easy walking can be done any time with little downside.

Use cardio as an adjustable lever during a cut. Rather than dropping calories ever lower as fat loss slows, you can add a little more walking or a short cardio session to widen the deficit while keeping food intake high enough to feel good and train hard.
